Bébé et enfant

Screen Time and Healthy Habits for Young Children

Mis à jour: July 1, 2026

Cet article est affiché en anglais en attendant sa traduction.

Screens are woven into modern family life, and pretending otherwise helps no one. The goal is not zero screens forever , it is making sure screens stay a small, intentional part of a childhood otherwise full of play, people, and sleep. Here is what general guidance says, translated into something a real family can actually do.

General guidance by age, in plain terms

Major health organizations land in roughly the same place. Under about 18 months to 2 years: avoid screen time apart from video calls with loved ones, which are interactive and genuinely valuable. Babies learn from faces, voices, and hands-on play , video mostly washes over them.

From around 2 to 5 years: aim for about an hour or less per day of good-quality content, ideally watched together. These are guideposts, not laws of physics , the direction (less, better, together) matters more than hitting an exact minute count on any given day.

Think of it less as a ration to enforce and more as protecting what screens displace: sleep, active play, conversation, and boredom , which is where imagination gets to work.

Quality beats quantity

Thirty minutes of a slow-paced, thoughtful show is a different experience from thirty minutes of frantic, algorithm-fed clips. Look for content that is calm in pace, tells an actual story, invites participation, and is made for your child’s age , and be wary of autoplay, which is designed to make stopping hard.

For toddlers, "educational" claims on apps deserve skepticism; most learning at this age happens through hands-on play and conversation. A decent rule of thumb: content your child could talk about afterward beats content that just flickers past.

Choosing specific shows or episodes , rather than open-ended scrolling , also builds in natural stopping points, which prevents half the battles before they start.

Watch together when you can

Co-viewing transforms screen time. When you watch alongside your child , naming things, asking "where did the bunny go?", connecting the story to their life ("You have a red truck too!") , the screen becomes a conversation starter instead of a babysitter.

Young children struggle to transfer what they see on a screen into real-world understanding on their own; a caregiver bridging the gap is what unlocks the learning. You do not need to co-view every minute of every show , that is not realistic , but making it the norm rather than the exception pays off.

Screen-free zones and times

A few firm boundaries do more work than constant minute-counting. Meals are the classic screen-free zone , for devices belonging to grown-ups too , because table conversation is where language, connection, and food habits grow.

The hour before bed is the other non-negotiable: screens are stimulating and light exposure can interfere with sleep, so end screen time well before the bedtime routine begins, and keep screens out of the bedroom. Backgrounds count too , a TV playing to nobody in particular measurably reduces how much families talk and how deeply children play, so switch it off when no one is truly watching.

Children copy what they see you do

Here is the uncomfortable part: children learn screen habits mostly by watching yours. A toddler who sees a parent scroll through every quiet moment learns that this is what humans do with quiet moments , no lecture can outweigh that demonstration.

You do not need to become a digital monk. Small, visible habits carry the message: putting the phone in another room during play time, narrating your use ("I am checking the map, then putting this away"), and following the same table rules you set for the kids.

Phones are also genuinely distracting in ways children notice , interactions get shorter and less responsive mid-scroll. Carving out phone-down stretches each day is one of the highest-value screen habits in the whole house, and it belongs to the adults.

Realistic, not perfect

Every family exceeds their screen ideals sometimes , on sick days, long flights, or the fourth video call of a workday. That is not failure; that is life. What shapes a childhood is the pattern across months, not the survival tactics of a rough Tuesday.

If current habits have drifted further than you would like, change them gradually , fewer contexts, better content, more co-viewing , rather than declaring a dramatic ban that nobody can sustain. Swapping in an appealing alternative works better than removal alone.

And drop the guilt. A warm, engaged home with imperfect screen habits beats a tense, guilt-ridden one with perfect ones. Aim for good patterns, forgive the exceptions, and keep the bigger picture in view: plenty of play, plenty of talk, plenty of sleep.

Points clés

  • Under ~2 years: skip screens apart from video calls; ages 2–5: aim for about an hour or less of quality content daily.
  • Quality and context beat minute-counting , calm, story-driven content chosen deliberately, not autoplay.
  • Co-viewing turns screens into conversation; young children learn far more with a caregiver alongside.
  • Protect meals and the hour before bed as screen-free, and turn off background TV.
  • Your own habits teach more than any rule , and imperfect weeks are normal, so skip the guilt.

Questions fréquentes

Are video calls with grandparents really okay for babies?

Yes , video chat is the standard exception to the "no screens under two" guidance because it is interactive and social: a responsive face talking to your baby, not content washing over them. It helps to join in and narrate the call for younger babies.

We went way over our screen limits this week. Have we done harm?

A heavy week , illness, travel, a work crunch , does not define your child’s development. What matters is the typical pattern over months. Simply return to your usual habits without drama, and skip the guilt spiral.

What is the best way to end screen time without a meltdown?

Give warnings before the end ("one more episode, then we are done"), use natural stopping points like the end of a show rather than mid-scene, and have the next activity ready to start. Consistency helps most , when the rule truly holds every time, children stop negotiating so hard.

Cet article relève de l’éducation générale et ne constitue ni un avis médical, ni un diagnostic, ni un traitement. Parlez toujours de votre situation à un professionnel de santé qualifié et, en cas d’urgence, consultez immédiatement.
